Mr. Miliband, you say you have discussed ending "Iran's aggression" with Marco Rubio. By what legal, moral, or humanitarian standard do you consider Iran the aggressor?

Two nuclear powers attacked Iran twice — in the middle of negotiations — and in the course of those attacks committed horrific war crimes:

- Bombing an elementary school in Minab during class hours, killing dozens of children;

- Attacking a sports hall in Lamerd during a girls' volleyball team practice;

- Firing on the Iranian vessel Dena in international waters as it returned from a naval parade hosted by India, killing around 100 unarmed sailors;

- Assassinating political leaders and scientists;

- Bombing civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, universities, bridges, petrochemical complexes, fuel depots, pharmaceutical factories, and desalination facilities;

- Bombing nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards.

The US president openly threatened to destroy a civilization so that it would "never rise again," at a time when the option of a diplomatic solution was within reach.

And you call these actions "Iran's aggression"?

Under General Assembly Resolution 3314, the party that initiates the use of force in violation of the UN Charter is considered the aggressor. Iran did not initiate the attack. You know this; your European counterparts know it too.

You had told your party that Britain's entry into the Iraq war was a mistake. That war, too, was justified by the false claim that weapons existed which did not exist at all. You more than anyone else should recognize this familiar scenario.

I challenge you to explain how a nation defending itself against two nuclear powers that threaten to destroy its civilization can be labeled an aggressor.

Did you also speak with Rubio about ending the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran? Or do you lack sufficient independence of judgment to raise such a question?

I wish it were the 1360s and I were seeking the dream of the embrace of martyrdom with the headband of Ya Zahra among the trenches. One day I will reach my beloved. My country's flag dances with joy in the sky. My people are proud of being Iranian. The sound of the adhan comes from the mosque and all become devoted, and from the God of their own selves, the Creator of their sufferings, they are freed and dissolve into the absolute good of existence... Perhaps here, perhaps elsewhere... A note for the professor...

"We and Gazprom": A Documentary Account of Why Iran's Gas Industry Fell Behind

The second episode of the "5 Khordad" podcast, titled "We and Gazprom," was screened today at the Atana Hotel in Tehran, attended by members of the Energy Commission of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, former and current energy officials, experts, and journalists. The documentary reviews Russia's experience in developing its gas industry to examine the obstacles facing the development of this industry in Iran and the role of Tehran-Moscow gas relations.

Focusing on the history of Russia's oil and gas industry, particularly the formation and expansion of the country's gas distribution network, the documentary seeks to examine the development paths of the gas industry in both Iran and Russia through the lens of historical experiences and strategic decisions.

In this episode, through conversations with veterans and experts of the gas industry, the question is raised: why has Iran, despite holding the world's second-largest natural gas reserves, been unable to develop its gas industry in proportion to its resource capacity and secure a more influential position in regional and global markets?

One of the documentary's central themes is the relationship between the abundance of gas resources, domestic pricing policy, and the development of gas industry infrastructure. Has the supply of cheap gas to consumers contributed to the sustainable development of this industry, or have pricing policies and rising domestic consumption constrained the resources needed for infrastructure investment and export development? The documentary seeks to examine various dimensions of this issue by presenting expert perspectives.

In another section, the documentary turns its attention to Iran-Russia gas relations—two countries that rank among the world's largest holders of natural gas reserves yet have taken different paths in developing gas exports. In this context, the question is raised: has Russia obstructed Iran's gas export development in recent years, and what impact has competition between the two countries had on Iran's export opportunities?

To watch the second episode of the "5 Khordad" podcast titled "We and Gazprom," follow the link below:

Data Colonialism The Data-Devouring of Tech Giants and…

Data Colonialism
The Data-Devouring of Tech Giants and Ways to Resist It
Analysis by Makhia, Nick Couldry
Translated by Hossein Sheikh-Rezaei
Science and Technology Studies Series / Director: Hossein Sheikh-Rezaei
356 pages / 1,250,000 Toman
View and purchase from the Kargadan website:
www.kargadanpub.com

🔸 Postcolonial studies centered on data and cyberspace help us understand that emerging technologies do not take shape in a social and political vacuum. Data, algorithms, and artificial intelligence, like any other technology, are constructed within power relations. The question is not "What technologies do we have?" but rather "Who designs them, what interests are involved in their deployment, and which groups benefit from their advantages and disadvantages?"

🔸 The authors of this book remind us that colonialism should not be defined merely in its historical form, including the occupation of territory and the creation of colonies. Colonialism has taken different forms throughout history and continues today in a new guise, including control over data extraction infrastructures and technological dependency. In the digital age, human data, social behaviors, and collective information have become resources that are collected from around the world and processed, accumulated, and made the basis for decision-making in a few centers.

🔸 The concept of "data colonialism" introduced by the authors of the book emphasizes precisely this aspect. The issue is not that data is inherently negative or that digital technology should be abandoned; the issue is that in the current global order, ownership and control of data are severely unbalanced and are mainly in the hands of large tech giants, who use it for profit, predicting collective behaviors, and even political influence.

🔸 In addition to theoretical analyses and case studies, the authors also propose solutions for countering data colonialism in the present era.

#Kargadan_Publishing, #New_Books, #Data_Colonialism, #Philosophy_of_Science, #Science_and_Technology_Studies

entry.title: [bamotamem] In the Motamem systems thinking discussion about Jared Diamond, one of the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

In the Motamem systems thinking discussion about Jared Diamond, one of the members had quoted something from Jared Diamond, and it occurred to me to write a bit there about his latest book, which was published last month. Naturally, there's more room for writing at length on Motamem. But still, I can share a few general points here as well:🖋️ In this book (and in almost all his books from the past thirty years), Diamond is pondering this question: which is greater — the power of "systems and structure" or the power of "people"?I think we Iranians are constantly thinking about this very question. That if so-and-so hadn't been there or hadn't come in such-and-such a year, or if someone else had come instead of someone else, how much would our historical trajectory have changed?🖋️ There are plenty of fascinating points and instructive stories in this book. But methodologically and analytically, I think it's weaker than Diamond's previous works. Still, by a wide margin, Guns, Germs, and Steel remains his best book.🖋️ Diamond believes in the power of influence for both individuals and systems. But he considers the effect of individuals greater in the short term and the effect of systems greater in the long term.🖋️ Diamond is old. One should always view the latest works of thinkers and writers with a forgiving eye. Because their goal is to deliver their remaining notes to us.
---

🔹One day a hunter went out to hunt and caught a deer. He picked up the deer's carcass and headed home. On the way, he came across a boar that attacked him.

🔹The hunter let an arrow fly and struck the boar on the temple; but as he was drawing his second arrow, the boar at that very moment dealt him a fatal wound and brought him down, and both died on the spot.

🔹A hungry wolf arrived at that plain and, seeing the bodies of the hunter, the deer, and the boar, was overcome with joy and said to himself: "Abundant provision has fallen to my lot, but the dictate of reason is to think of the future and not be greedy; I will hide and store the fresh meats so that I may live carefree for a long time, and today I will content myself with chewing only the leather and the bowstring."

The clock of Hormuz was set against the enemy
🔹In a siege, time is a scarce commodity — because the enemy has targeted your resilience, not merely your soil or your fleet.
🔹Every day of delay deepens the attrition. So the besieged actor must not manage time; it must turn time into a weapon.
🔹The lesson of history is that in asymmetric balances, victory takes shape in the opponent's mind before the battlefield.
🔸Now the enemy must be brought to understand that no scenario — neither maximum pressure nor limited operations — leads to victory. This is the premise of sustainable peace.
🔹The shift in the pattern of tension in the Strait of Hormuz must now be read within this same framework. Striking a ship's propulsion, dealing firmly with Emirati vessels, punishing ships that turn off AIS — these are not merely tactics; they are messages.
🔹The Strait of Hormuz now plays the role of a clock. Every action must make the cost of passage outweigh the profit of victory and drown the opponent's will in the calculation of defeat.
🔹The main danger, however, is the pulse of negotiation at a moment when the perception of non-victory has not yet taken hold in the enemy.
🔹A signal of dialogue under these conditions is no free lunch, and it can muddy the message of power and hand time back to the opponent's favor.
🔹In a siege, trial and error is a luxury. Iran must compress time, not sell it off through hesitation. Peace comes when the opponent comes to believe that victory is impossible.
@Farsna - Link

Saudi Arabia's Deadlock in the War with Yemen

🔹A British magazine has written about the worsening of Saudi Arabia's security crisis following missile strikes by the Yemeni army on Riyadh airport and the failure of the counterattack by the country's allied forces in Yemen — a situation that, beyond casting doubt on Saudi Arabia's military capability, also threatens Bin Salman's economic ambitions.

Saudi Arabia's Defenseless Skies

🔸The Economist writes that the reasons behind the failure of Saudi Arabia's air defense systems to intercept the missiles that struck Riyadh airport remain unclear. This comes even as Saudi Arabia is equipped with advanced American "THAAD" and "Patriot" systems. Saudi Arabia is also worried about the depletion of its interceptor missile stockpiles.

The Counterattack Has Hit a Dead End

🔹The halt of the Saudis' advance 40 kilometers south of the port of Al-Mokha shows that stagnation has once again returned to the battlefield. At the same time, Yemeni army forces are trying to besiege the city of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city and one of the most important strongholds of Saudi-affiliated forces.

Saudi Arabia's Economic Losses from the Ongoing War

🔸The organizers of the "Future Investment Initiative" conference — one of the most important international events used by Bin Salman to attract major investors — announced only a few hours before Saturday's attack that they were prepared to hold the event on October 26. But the recent attacks have raised questions about whether participants can travel to Riyadh and whether they are willing to attend the meeting.

Negotiation: A Costly Option for Riyadh

🔹The Economist sees negotiation with Sana'a as an alternative option, but predicts that the Yemeni government will demand a heavy political and economic price in exchange for halting the attacks.

🔹The British magazine goes on to write that the Yemenis, compared to Saudi Arabia, have a greater capacity to endure a long war. Saudi Arabia, by contrast, faces direct threats against its investments, airports, and energy sector — threats that also jeopardize the country's plans to become a regional hub for tourism and business.

They proposed to him: "Do not hunt anymore and do not trouble yourself; we will draw lots every day and send one animal to your presence as your daily food." The lion accepted, and matters continued this way for a while.🔹One day the lot of death fell to the rabbit. The other animals wanted to send him off, but the rabbit cleverly said: "If you give me time and let me proceed with my own plan, I will rid you of this lion forever." The animals agreed.🔹The rabbit deliberately took a roundabout way and delayed so much that the lion's lunchtime passed, and the lion became furious and restless from extreme hunger. Near sunset, the rabbit went to the lion with a frightened appearance and in haste. The lion roared and said: "Where are you coming from, and why are you late? Why have the animals sent such a small and insignificant prey for me?"🔹The rabbit said: "O king! We were coming to you together with another rabbit that was fat and large; but on the way, another lion blocked our path and snatched that rabbit. No matter how much I said this is an offering for the sultan of this thicket, he said: I am the true king of this land, and I will destroy that boastful lion!"🔹The lion became angry and shouted: "Where is he? Show me his location!" entry.title: [VahidOnline] Shahrzad Shahbazi, one of the lawyers for the defendants in the "Aliakhani…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @VahidOnline

Shahrzad Shahbazi, one of the lawyers for the defendants in the "Aliakhani Square of Isfahan" case and the lawyer for Alireza Sepahi, has rejected the narrative put forward by state media, announcing that the charge of killing law enforcement officers was never communicated to any of the defendants in this case, nor did the court address this charge. So far, five of the defendants in this case have been executed, and seven others remain at risk of execution. The lawyer's statements came in response to the publication of an interview in state media in which a woman, introduced as the wife of one of the killed officers, accuses the defendants of killing and burning officers. The interview was published after criticism mounted over the carrying out of executions, particularly the execution of Alireza Sepahi. Shahbazi also questioned the presence of this woman at the site of the executions, asking: when the case did not involve qisas or a personal right, on what basis was she allowed to be present at the site where the sentence was carried out? In a message posted on Instagram on Saturday, 18 Mehr 1405, Shahbazi wrote: "The charge of killing has under no circumstances been communicated to any of the defendants in the Aliakhani Square and Shohada Square case." She emphasized that the allegation of "burning officers in connection with premeditated murder" was neither addressed in court nor included among the charges in the verdict. Shahbazi cited the Revolutionary Court's lack of jurisdiction over this charge as the reason it did not take up the matter of killing. The Aliakhani Square case was opened after four Special Unit officers were killed during the protests of 18 Dey 1404 in Isfahan. State media had previously published videos of the defendants' confessions during interrogations, crime scene reconstructions, and trial sessions in Branch One of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court — confessions that human rights bodies consider forced and invalid. Alireza Sepahi was executed in the early hours of Monday, 13 Mehr. Mai Sato, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran, in reaction to the execution, had reported serious concerns about the torture of defendants and the lack of a fair trial in this case. According to Sato, the sentence was carried out while Sepahi's lawyer was still working to have the case reviewed. Sepahi had previously also been on the verge of public execution, but was transferred to the hospital after a heart attack. That same night, citizens stayed in Aliakhani Square until dawn to prevent the executions from being carried out.@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [darvishnameh] Shahvar!✍Yaser Arab For fifteen years, they cut down the trees, slashed the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

Shahvar!✍Yaser Arab
For fifteen years, they cut down the trees, slashed the bushes, displaced the animals, destroyed the birds' nests, and carved up the body of Mount Shahvar — this source of water, bread, and life for the people — and most of us just watched, without understanding what was being lost!

Some thought, what does one mountain matter? What harm could it do to take a piece of a mountain?

They didn't understand that Shahvar is not just stone, not just a home for bears, not just a shelter for birds, not just the memory of the forest — but a part of the life cycle on which the life of the plains, agriculture, and the people of Bastam and Shahroud depend, to which they are bound.

Those who saw the stone but not the water, who saw the mine but not the land. Those who failed to understand that the wound being inflicted today on the body of Mount Shahvar can tomorrow turn into the thirst of the earth, the pollution of water, and the endless suffering of the people — they must be held accountable today!

Now Shahvar remains; wounded and silent. A Shahvar that seems to have become a Shahzar for years, weeping bitterly to itself.

But it is no longer time for mourning alone. It is time to stand, time to ask, time to demand answers from those who allowed this wound to deepen every day for fifteen years!

@yaser_arab57

entry.title: [mostafamalekian] 🔴I Have Not Been Happy ✍️ From an interview with Mostafa Malekian.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴I Have Not Been Happy ✍️ From an interview with Mostafa Malekian. Published in Andishe Pouya 102

You have always said that spirituality is a process that brings tranquility, joy, and hope. As you pass seventy, have you yourself attained this tranquility, joy, and hope?

🔹As for tranquility, I am content and I believe I have it. As for hope, I am also content. But joy, no. From childhood onward, I think — perhaps due to my psychological makeup, or perhaps due to my childhood environment — I have fundamentally never been happy. This one thing I truly lack, and I have never truly laughed from the bottom of my heart; never.

Looking back on your life from the vantage point of seventy, what was the hardest period of your life? And what was the most precious price you paid for intellectual honesty?

🔹I think the most precious price I paid was losing friends. I am a person who cherishes friendship, and friendship matters greatly to me. To this day, I myself have never cut ties with anyone. But with every intellectual transformation I underwent, I lost a number of friends for whom I was very dear. It was as though their beliefs mattered more to them, and when I changed my beliefs, they would sever their friendship with me.

🔹The hardest period of my life was when I forsook many outward trappings and privileges in order to bring about, in my own estimation, a transformation in the Qom seminary. At that time I was also devout in every sense; out of compassion and mercy, I wanted the educational, training, and research system of the seminary to change so that the very goals they held would be realized and achieved in the best possible way. For example, I myself began changing the textbooks — that is, I was teaching, but not with the seminary textbooks, rather with books I deemed better. But gradually I saw that I was far too small to accomplish anything against this very old edifice. During those eighteen years in which I wanted to do something in Qom, I was awarded a scholarship twice to be sent abroad, and I went neither time. It always seemed to me that if this transformation took place in the seminaries, it would be more beneficial for society. But I returned unsuccessful. In the year 1372, after much pressure, I came and bought a house in Tehran and returned to Tehran to live. Again some of the gentlemen insisted that no, stay in the seminary. I gave back the very house I had bought in Tehran, and returned to Qom once more, staying there another seven years until the year 1379. But I saw that everything was falling apart.

@andishepouya
@mostafamalekian

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Some people only see and touch the ground they were standing on after they fall.

First explanation

In the early years of Motamem, when we started the daily sentences, sometimes I would also put some of my own words among the daily sentences at the top of the site.

After a while, I felt it wasn't a nice thing to do. The people whose words we were quoting were great people; thinkers, opinion-makers, and at the very least, well-known. Putting my own words among those people's words wasn't a nice thing to do.

I have no problem with saying and writing my words separately (I've been busy with exactly that my whole life). But that thing wasn't mature. In short, consider the photo-note above as the youthful transgressions caused by rawness.

Second explanation

Eleven years ago, when I gave a talk about personal branding, I ended my speech with a sentence that I still like and still stand by. Since the underlying theme of that sentence was also falling, it came to mind now:

Not everyone falls downward,
some fall upward.

#جمله‌های_روزانه_متمم

The Wall Street Journal also reported, citing Saudi officials, that missiles fired by the Houthis struck Terminal 3 of the airport directly. A hospital source told Agence France-Presse that five of the wounded are in intensive care. An eyewitness also said that while at Gate 403 of the domestic flights terminal, he saw a missile strike the area of Gate 401 and passengers being wounded. The witness told Agence France-Presse: "I saw Gate 401 being hit and people wounded before my eyes. Everyone was fleeing." Saturday's attack came after Riyadh airport had already been targeted by Houthi attacks on Wednesday and Thursday. Those attacks left a total of four dead and several wounded, and caused serious damage to a passenger plane belonging to a Saudi airline. Three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in Thursday's attacks, and one Sudanese citizen in Wednesday's attack. The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks. entry.summary:

Source: @darvishnameh

Superadobe is an expanded method of the same old adobe, using long bags filled with moistened soil and then tamped down for proper compaction. The bags are stacked row by row in a circular plan, rising uniformly to form a dome. To prevent the bags from shifting and also to resist earthquakes, barbed wire is used between the layers, acting like mortar to bind the rows together and helping give the structure an integrated, chain-like quality that gives it high resistance to earthquakes and other events. In this structure, due to the dome form, the thickness of the walls, and the natural materials used, heat exchange with the outside is minimized and energy loss is managed dramatically. Superadobe was invented by Nader Khalili, an Iranian architect, and is now recognized worldwide as one of the methods for building sustainable and natural homes. Will Iran launch a preemptive strike before the American election? In Washington, this scenario is being taken seriously. The logic goes like this: Tehran's clock is an hourglass, and every day the sanctions erode the economy further. If Tehran is certain that after November 2 it will be attacked regardless, waiting means losing. So the best moment to strike is a few weeks before the election. Iran would both demonstrate its power and knock Trump down at the ballot box, because any response from America would drag the war into the middle of election season. But this calculation has one big hole: January 3, the day the new American Congress begins its work. From November 2 until that day, Trump is neither worried about votes nor dealing with a new Congress. On the other side, until the election, Trump sees any war as harmful to himself and buys time. Every day he buys time is an advantage for Tehran and reduces the incentive to preempt. So everything comes back to a question that James Fearon has called the "commitment problem": Does Tehran believe that after the election it will not be attacked? If it believes so, preemption makes no sense. If it does not, Schelling's dark room may at any moment ring out with the sound of gunfire.@sadegh_alhosseini

Excerpts from my recent interview with the IBNA book news agency: "If Sohrab were alive today, in the third millennium and in today's Tehran, and were present at his exhibitions, which part of what he had to say would be more worth hearing, and what would your first question to him be?" In my view, Sohrab's calmness, composure, and Stoic way of being would take on great significance; a subject about which much could be said separately. This calmness manifests in his lovemaking with and proximity to nature and a kind of "ataraxia," meaning inner tranquility, which the Stoic philosophers spoke about. Sohrab had internalized this calmness and also looked upon the world with a poetic gaze. The critique of technology, which I spoke about earlier, death-awareness and the effort to give meaning to life are also among the hearable and contemporary parts of his thought. Loving nature, paying attention to the other, and reflecting on categories such as death, love, solitude, and suffering can, in my view, still be worth hearing today. Regarding the exhibition of his paintings that you mentioned, naturally the paintings themselves matter; but I think Sohrab's words about the world and his way of living are also very important today. The reason is that in his case, there was considerable overlap between his public and private life, between his lived life and his work. He lived the way he wrote, and especially the way he composed poetry. This overlap and what we call "authenticity" can make a person charismatic and influence others; an unpretentious and intimate influence, such that one could benefit from his company and not feel the passage of time. In such conditions, the person's own presence and way of living become as important as his words. If I want to answer your question, "If you saw Sohrab, what would your first question to him be?" The truth is, I might not have had any specific question at all. For more than thirty years I have been living in Sohrab's atmosphere. Perhaps I would have liked to watch him; or, to put it better, to spend time in his company from noon until night, to chat together and experience that composure and calmness that was in his being, in socializing with him. I wanted to benefit, to the extent of my capacity, from that calmness that I believe had descended upon him. Sohrab himself said: "We ourselves are the awning of our calmness." I would have liked to catch and experience a breeze of that composure and calmness from his company... entry.title: [fazelimohammadir] A man of building ▪️ Mohsen Khalili Iraqi passed away today, 17 Mehr 1405.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @fazelimohammadir

A man of building ▪️ Mohsen Khalili Iraqi passed away today, 17 Mehr 1405. A man whose name was intertwined with industry, entrepreneurship, and resilience. His passing marks the loss of one of the enduring figures of Iran's industry. An industrialist whose life demonstrated that building a factory is only the beginning of the journey, and that the greater art lies in keeping it alive through difficult times and passing it on to future generations. ▪️ Khalili Iraqi, born in 1308, grew up in a family where work and initiative held a special place. His father, Mahmoud Khalili, was one of the pioneers of Iran's industry, and Mohsen set out alongside him on a path that led to the founding of Butan. Father and son saw an opportunity to improve people's lives in the gases that flared above the oil wells. The fruit of this vision was the expansion of liquid gas use and subsequently the production of gas appliances, which wove industry into the daily lives of Iranian families. ▪️ He belonged to a generation that saw industry as a path to the nation's prosperity. Involvement in industrial associations and efforts to strengthen cooperation among producers formed another part of his legacy. In this vision, the progress of one factory was inseparable from the fate of other enterprises, and defending production required cooperation and organization among industrialists. His professional life, of course, was not without hardship. After the revolution, part of Butan's shares were subject to confiscation orders, and the Khalili family struggled for years to reclaim them. From what I have heard, Mohsen Khalili appeared in court 254 times to win back his company. He and his partners, in order to keep the company afloat and pay the workers' wages, even sold their personal properties. This act of standing firm is one of the brightest chapters of his life. ▪️ In his final years, the concern for development never left his mind. He dedicated part of his wealth to industrial research, and through the establishment of the Mohsen Khalili Iraqi Industrial Development Foundation, he supported the study of the challenges of Iran's industrialization. Supporting economists' research was a continuation of the very path he had begun decades earlier in the workshop and the factory. An effort to find ways to build a more prosperous Iran. From the bottom of my heart, I offer my condolences to the honorable family and friends of Engineer Khalili on his passing. May his soul rest in peace and his memory be cherished ☑️ Mohsen Jalalpour mohsenjalalpour

The historical instance of this view can also be found in history. In Book Five of the History of the Peloponnesian War, written by Thucydides, the dialogue between the Melians and the Athenians is detailed.

The story was that in 416 BC, Athens asked the small island of Melos to surrender to its empire. The Melians tried to maintain their neutrality and hoped that justice, independence, and the possibility of help from Sparta would protect them, but the Athenians stated their argument clearly:

"The issue is not only our present enemies; independent islands like you are also a danger to the empire, because they stand outside our order... if peoples maintain their independence, it is because they have power; and if we do not attack them, it is because we fear them. So by subjugating you, in addition to expanding our empire, we also increase our security; especially since you are islanders and weaker than others and should not be able to prevail over the masters of the sea."

With Love and Without Love

"Duty without love becomes tedious; duty performed with love makes one steadfast. Responsibility without love makes one inconsiderate; responsibility borne with love makes one caring. Justice without love makes one hard-hearted; justice practiced with love makes one trustworthy. Upbringing without love becomes contentious; upbringing carried out with love makes one patient. Wisdom without love makes one cunning; wisdom exercised with love makes one understanding. Kindness without love becomes hypocritical; kindness shown with love makes one benevolent. Order without love leads to fault-finding; order upheld with love makes one open-minded. Knowledge and expertise without love make one self-righteous; knowledge and expertise applied with love make one trustworthy. Power without love makes one violent; power wielded with love makes one helpful. Dignity without love makes one arrogant; dignity upheld with love makes one humble. Wealth without love makes one miserly; wealth used with love makes one generous. Faith without love makes one fanatical; faith lived with love makes one peaceable."

Source: unknown author; as cited in Hans Küng, Was ich glaube, München: Piper Verlag, 2009, pp. 268–269. Translated from the German text. [Sourcing and translation by artificial intelligence]

"Duty without love makes one peevish; duty fulfilled in love makes one constant. Responsibility without love makes one ruthless; responsibility borne in love makes one caring. Justice without love makes one hard; justice practiced in love makes one reliable. Upbringing without love makes one contradictory; upbringing undertaken in love makes one patient. Cleverness without love makes one cunning; cleverness practiced in love makes one understanding. Friendliness without love makes one hypocritical; friendliness shown in love makes one kind. Order without love makes one petty; order maintained in love makes one generous. Expertise without love makes one opinionated; expertise exercised in love makes one trustworthy. Power without love makes one violent; power employed in love makes one helpful. Honor without love makes one haughty; honor preserved in love makes one modest. entry.title: [VahidOnline] Margaret Hamilton, an American scientist and one of the pioneers of software…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @VahidOnline

Margaret Hamilton, an American scientist and one of the pioneers of software engineering who played a key role in landing the first American astronauts on the Moon, has died at the age of 90. She led a team of experts who designed and developed the software used in NASA's Apollo space missions. MIT, confirming Hamilton's death, announced that she passed away on Wednesday, the eighth of Mehr 1405, corresponding to September 30, 2026. In a statement, the institute described Hamilton as one of the pioneers of computer science who played an important role in developing the field before software engineering became a widespread profession. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and headed the software engineering division. The group she managed designed the guidance and control software for the Apollo 11 spacecraft, which played a decisive role in the historic landing of Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon in 1969. During this mission, the spacecraft's computer encountered a processing overload moments before landing, but the software designed by Hamilton's group was able to continue the landing operation by prioritizing tasks. Barack Obama, the former president of the United States, awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 in recognition of Hamilton's scientific achievements and her role in advancing space technology. @VahidOOnLine📡 @VahidOnline

entry.summary:

Source: @VahidOnline

Reuters reported on Thursday, 16 Mehr, that the number of ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to its lowest level in more than two months, following a surge in attacks on oil tankers last week. Citing data and analysis from the analytics firm Kpler, Reuters reported that only 7 commercial vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday — the lowest figure since the first of Mordad. Crude oil transit through the strait also dropped 27 percent from the wartime peak the previous week, falling to at least 10.1 million barrels per day, equivalent to 74 percent of the pre-war level. According to Kpler analysts, most of this decline is attributable to ship-to-ship transfers of cargoes in the Sea of Oman. According to Reuters, however, exports from the coasts of the Sea of Oman and the Red Sea rose to 6.7 million barrels per day — more than double the pre-war level — helping to offset the reduced supply through the Strait of Hormuz. Kpler data shows the number of transiting ships rose to 10 on Wednesday, but remained far below the more than 20 vessels seen on Sunday and Monday. The report comes after attacks on oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz last week reached their highest weekly level since the start of the Iran war. Before the war began on the ninth of Esfand last year, roughly 125 large commercial ships — including oil tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, and container ships — passed through the Strait of Hormuz daily. Meanwhile, Donald Trump, the President of the United States, posted a chart on Thursday on the Truth Social network showing that oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to levels seen before the US and Israeli war against Iran.@VahidOOnLine📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [jalaeipour] "He was so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness."…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

"He was so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness."

In his autobiography, the late Arthur Arberry writes of the late Reynold A. Nicholson — scholar, commentator, and translator of literary and mystical works from Persian and Arabic into English:

He was a consummate scholar, so enamored of his books that he sacrificed his eyesight to ceaseless reading, so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness. In the final years of his life, when the lamp of his eyes was flickering toward extinction, he composed this verse — a poem that, to me, among all the last words ever uttered by human beings, carries the truest inspiration and the most moving farewell:

When Truth appears unveiled before your eyes,
These tongues are left bewildered and surprised.
*I shall fall silent — the Beloved has come to speak:*
*Listen, and God knows best what is right and true.*
*Become devoid of sense, of hearing, and of thought,*
*That you may hear the summons "Return!"*
As long as this tongue remains, you shall not hear the Word.
So words must be brief. And peace.

**I have borrowed the Persian rendering of Nicholson's poem from verses of the Masnavi. The asterisked lines are from the Masnavi.

- Nicholson's poem, as narrated by Arberry, reads:
When Truth shines out words fail and nothing tell;
Now hear the Voice within your hearts. Farewell.

This is the closing verse of a long poem that Arberry quoted and confirmed earlier in this same piece, noting that in these verses Nicholson was deeply influenced by Rumi: ... He seldom spoke of his personal beliefs, and I, too, in twenty-five years of close friendship with him, learned little about how he was raised or of his spiritual journey. Yet the image that took shape in my mind was that he, like many others, had lost his faith in youth and then recovered it through intellectual companionship and kinship of spirit with Muslim mystics.

In his old age, he composed a poem in which, for the first time, he laid bare his innermost thoughts. It was clear that these thoughts had been profoundly shaped by long years of studying Rumi's works ...

Mohammad Mehdi Mojahedi
16 Mehr 1405
@mmojahedi

entry.summary:

Source: @Kayhan_online

Kayhan investigates 🔰 Securing gas for the northern provinces is one of the president's goals on his trip to Turkmenistan

🔸With the onset of the cold season, the gas imbalance will become apparent, especially in the north of the country; therefore, the president, who is heading to Turkmenistan today, must pursue the import and swap of gas from the northern neighbor.

🔸According to our reporter, our country, due to its vast geography and the unparalleled coverage of the household gas network, along with the dependence of power plants and various industries on gas fuel, has faced an imbalance between production and consumption. The enemy's attack on South Pars during the 40-day war, although it met with Iran's decisive and unexpected response to the gas facilities of "Ras Laffan" and caught the enemy off guard, part of the country's gas production was also damaged and the imbalances worsened.

🔸Damage to five phases of the South Pars refineries during the Ramadan war reduced the country's daily gas production capacity by about 230 million cubic meters. So far, according to the National Gas Company, 95 million cubic meters of gas have returned to the grid, and currently there is a deficit of 135 million cubic meters of gas.

🔸If the upcoming winter is similar to last year's winter in terms of temperature and consumption, and only 95 million cubic meters of the damaged capacity is restored, the gas deficit will be about 130 million cubic meters, which, combined with the previous imbalance figure, will total about 380 million cubic meters per day.

🔸The gas shortage problem is not limited to homes, and power plants, in order to prevent power outages for household subscribers, are forced to turn to alternative fuels, namely diesel and fuel oil. The increased consumption of fuel oil, or mazut, also leads to an increase in pollutants and worsening air pollution.

🔸Of course, gas imports from Turkmenistan also face obstacles. The story of gas imports from this country began with a 25-year contract concluded between the parties in 1997, but due to financial problems that arose during Bijan Zangeneh's ministry in Hassan Rouhani's government, it ran into trouble in subsequent years. Of course, the other side also had breaches of commitment, which ultimately, with the weak defense of the Iranian side in the legal dispute, resulted in our country being fined. This fine and its consequences have cast a shadow over oil transfers between the two countries in recent years.

🔸Despite all these problems, during the era of the martyred Raisi in the Thirteenth Government and with Iran's personal follow-up, Iran was able to receive the right of oil swap between Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan in the form of gas. Now the Fourteenth Government must exert all its power to renew this matter — whether in the form of swap rights or direct import.

entry.title: [mostafamalekian] 🔴How can we make the most of middle age? We shouldn't expect our past selves…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴How can we make the most of middle age? We shouldn't expect our past selves to have our present understanding. ✍Mostafa Malekian

Sometimes we look at the past and say: If I had spent those years doing something else, I would have a better life today. Why did I play so much as a child? Why did I pursue things in my youth that no longer matter to me today?

But in this judgment, we forget one thing: every period of life has its own demands. We cannot have had a childhood without having the interests and desires of childhood. We cannot have gone through youth and yet expect to have had our present maturity from the very beginning.

Part of our sorrow about the past comes from this very expectation — as if we wanted to have been as mature throughout our entire lives as we are today. Whereas it is precisely by going through those periods that we have reached this point.

▪️ Let us not see past mistakes as pure loss

Even a choice that we consider a mistake today may have brought us joys and friendships.

For example, we say, why did I pursue football instead of studying? But how much happiness has that same football given us? What friendships did it create that have stayed with us later in life?

If we only look at the costs of a choice and dismiss all the good things that came from it, we will not have a complete picture of the past.

▪️ No life is all benefit and no cost

Every way of life opens up possibilities before us and also carries costs. We cannot compare our lived life with an imaginary life that has all the good things and pays no price for them.

▪️ Let us seize the remaining opportunities

Not all opportunities are lost with the end of youth. There are still things we can begin, things we can learn, and pleasures we can experience.

If we spend today only on regret for yesterday, in a few more years, today will also become a new subject for regret.

Instead of only lamenting lost opportunities, let us treasure the opportunities not yet lost.

📚 Mostafa Malekian | Lecture on the book "Philosophical Guidance for Middle Age"
@mostafamalekian

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sadegh_alhosseini

The real barrel is $31 more expensive than the paper barrel!Sadegh Al-HosseiniThe chart above shows the price gap between physical oil cargoes and futures contracts. The physical cargo is the same "dated Brent" that is loaded in the North Sea today. The futures contract is the number we hear in the news as the oil price. Under normal conditions this gap is small, but today it has reached $31.That means when the futures contract trades at around $100, a refinery that needs real oil today pays about $131.The peak of this gap came during the war and on Farvardin 20 of this year, when it reached nearly $36. In Tir it even turned negative, and now it has once again approached the record.The paper market trades on hope: a deal, calmer seas, and the end of the crisis. The physical market trades on the barrel that either exists or doesn't. One of the two has to give. Either the shortage is resolved, or the paper price climbs toward the real price.In short, the paper market has pinned its hopes on the end of the crisis, but the physical market won't be won over by hope! It has to keep its refinery's wheels turning!@sadegh_alhosseini

If the government or other institutions have such resources at their disposal, are their hands tied that Alireza Zakani should use their money to drum up political publicity for himself? entry.title: [sadegh_alhosseini] Oil transit through Hormuz rises: The White House celebrated, the market didn't…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sadegh_alhosseini

Oil transit through Hormuz rises: The White House celebrated, the market didn't buy it
Sadegh Al-Hosseini
Kelley Vlahos, editor of Responsible Statecraft, made important points in yesterday's article that I'll get into below. He says last week the White House and its supporters announced "the strait is open and we've won." On Sunday, however, Brent was still holding at $102. The gap between these two images is what this article is about.
What's really going on behind the numbers? Daily oil transit through Hormuz has reached 13 to 17 million barrels, down from about 20 million before the war. But a large portion of it is happening through an emergency workaround: state-owned ships pass through the strait with their tracking systems turned off and hand off their cargo to supertankers in safe waters. The cost of chartering a supertanker from the Persian Gulf to Asia has hit $1.2 million, insurance has gotten more expensive, and ships carrying fertilizer, aluminum, petrochemicals, and grain are still stranded in the Persian Gulf. America has sent a third aircraft carrier to the region, and its navy is, according to experts, stretched thin.
The drawdown from reserves is also heavy: 400 million barrels drawn from reserves in March, another 100 million barrels from the G7, America's strategic reserves at their lowest level since 1983, and JPMorgan saying it sees no end to this situation.
In other words, Iran can't fully close the strait, and America can't fully open it. Unless Trump reaches a deal with Iran; that's what the market is really waiting for.
Why is this news encouraging for us?
1. Trump's leverage has hit its ceiling. With three aircraft carriers, the strait has only become "half-open." When American experts themselves say the only way out is a deal with Iran, it means the military option costs more than it delivers.
2. The clock is working against the White House. The November midterm elections are approaching, and according to experts, fuel prices won't come down by then; the soaring cost of diesel has even hit American farmers. This pressure raises the incentive for a deal. But it's clear that the cost of this war is being paid by the people of Iran.
3. A deal would untie many knots at once. A world whose reserves have run dry is thirsty for fresh supply; it's not just oil — petrochemicals, fertilizer, and metals are also stuck behind this barrier.
The world has come to believe that Hormuz today is neither closed nor open; and the key is not on warships but on the negotiating table.
Full text of the article: https://responsiblestatecraft.org/hormuz-oil-transits-war/

[FarsNA] A mouth that opened at the wrong time
🔹In a clear pond, two ducks and a…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @FarsNA

A mouth that opened at the wrong time

🔹In a clear pond, two ducks and a turtle were neighbors, and a deep friendship and bond had formed between them. Time passed, and due to drought, the water in the pond began to dry up.

🔹The ducks, seeing that it was no longer possible to stay, came to the turtle to say goodbye and migrate to another body of water.

🔹The turtle lamented with sorrow and tears and said: "Waterlessness is far more dangerous for me, a slow-moving animal, than for you, and my life is impossible without any water. It is not the way of chivalry that you abandon me in this waterlessness; think of me and take me along with you."

🔹The ducks said: "Being apart from you is hard for us too, but you have a flaw: you take the advice of friends lightly and you don't shut your mouth at the right time!

🔹If you want us to take you too, there is one condition: we will bring a stick, we two will hold its two ends in our beaks, and you hold the middle of the stick firmly with your mouth so we can take flight. In the sky, no matter what people say and whatever shouts they raise, do not open your mouth!"

🔹The turtle promised and said: "I will obey and will not open my lips until the destination."

🔹The ducks brought the stick, the turtle gripped its middle firmly with its teeth, and they leapt into the air. As they were passing over a village, people's eyes fell on this amazing scene. An uproar rose among the people and they shouted: "Look! How the ducks are carrying the turtle through the air with a stick!"

🔹Hearing the clamor, the turtle could not endure it and became angry. Thinking it would say something to them, it opened its mouth and said: "May your eyes be blinded!"

🔹But as soon as it opened its lips, the stick was released from its mouth, and it fell from the height of the sky to the ground.

#حکایت@Farsna

You can listen to the recording of the launch event for Fukuyama's new book, titled "In the Realm of the Last Man," recently held at the London School of Economics and Political Science, here (file). The book traces the trajectory of his life, his positions, and his intellectual evolution over the past five decades. In it, Fukuyama explains how, under the influence of political and economic developments, he moved beyond the theory of the "End of History" and no longer sees the future of liberal democracy as guaranteed. Once known as one of the ideologues of the American right, he now considers himself a social democrat and stresses the need for wealth redistribution and stronger labor unions. He says he held two deep beliefs, both of which have been undermined by the developments of recent years: the belief that American military intervention can help spread democracy, and the belief in a maximally free market. The results of the American military attack on Iraq shattered the first belief, and the 2008 financial crisis shattered the second. He sees the rise of Trump in America as a sign of democracy's fragile state in the free market, and stresses that societies must have credible institutions to regulate the market and preserve democracy's institutional capacities.

🔴 Four differences between morality and religious rituals and rites✍Mostafa Malekian🔹Why are religious rulings and rituals not among moral requirements? Because moral propositions and ritual religious propositions differ from one another, including:▪️ 1. Rational justificationMoral rulings are capable of rational justification; one can explain what effect observing or not observing them has on human life.For example, reason understands that lying destroys trust, misleads others in decision-making, and damages human relationships. But reason alone does not understand what problems human life in general would face if we did not perform wudu or tayammum.▪️ 2. The bond among human beingsMorality can serve as the basis of a shared system for the life of all human beings; a system that helps their coexistence and compatibility. But rituals and rites do not create such a universal commonality and can also mark the boundary between followers of different religions and sects.▪️ 3. Conscience versus instructionMorality is related to the inner conscience of the human being; a person feels within themselves that good is preferable to evil. But knowledge of rituals and rites depends on instruction and cultural transmission.Imagine a fourteen-year-old adolescent who has not received religious instruction: they can understand the meaning of honesty — that is, harmony among beliefs, feelings, desires, speech, and action — and grasp its value; but they do not know prayer, tayammum, or the Eucharist without instruction.▪️ 4. Stability versus historical dependenceMoral values are not specific to a particular time, geography, ethnicity, or nation; but the form of rituals and rites depends on historical and cultural contexts.For example, the form and limits of religious covering and what is considered hijab have not been the same in different periods and societies. Ways of worship also differ among religious traditions. But the value of honesty does not change with a change of clothing, land, or historical period; harmony of speech and action and not deceiving others still has moral value.➖An excerpt from a private conversation among friends - Dey 96@mostafamalekian

The Islamic Republic has executed Alireza Sepahi, one of those detained during the Dey 1404 protests.
- The "Mizan" news agency, affiliated with the judiciary of the Islamic Republic, reported that Alireza Sepahi Badjani, known as Alireza Sepahi, was executed at dawn on Monday, 13 Mehr 1405, in Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan.
- Alireza Sepahi's lawyer had warned the previous day of the imminent danger of his execution, announcing that Sepahi's family had been summoned to meet with him and that he had been transferred to solitary confinement.
- Before his execution, Alireza Sepahi married his fiancée by telephone. Mahshad Kashani, a 22-year-old student living in Isfahan, was also arrested during the Dey 1404 protests and sentenced to five years of discretionary imprisonment; she is being held in the women's prison in Dolatabad, Isfahan.
- Alireza Sepahi had been scheduled to be executed at dawn on Tuesday, 6 Mordad 1405, alongside Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani — his cousin — and Amirhossein Safari Hosseinabadi, in Malek Shahr, Isfahan, in a public execution, but he suffered a heart attack from stress before the sentence could be carried out, and his execution was postponed.
- Alireza Sepahi is the fourth citizen arrested during the Dey 1404 protests to be executed over the past week, following the issuance of a statement by 46 countries condemning executions in Iran. Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi was executed on Saturday, 11 Mehr, in Shahrekord, and Ali Hemmati Sistani and Majid Nikandish were executed on Wednesday, 8 Mehr, in Mashhad.
- The case known as the "Midan Alikhani" case is connected to the protests on the evening of 18 Dey 1404, which took place in the area of Midan Alikhani, between Malek Shahr and Kaveh in Isfahan. The security institutions of the Islamic Republic claimed that four Basij and special unit forces were killed during these protests.
- With the execution of Alireza Sepahi, six defendants in the "Midan Alikhani" case have now been executed. Erfan Esfandiari and Golmohammad Mohammadi were executed on 28 Tir in prison. Abolfazl Sepahi and Amirhossein Safari were hanged in public on 6 Mordad in "Midan Alikhani," and Ghaem Hosseini was executed on 29 Mordad in the Central Prison of Isfahan (Dastgerd).

📝 "On the occasion of Paknejad's farewell"

🔹 In every government, there's always a fight over who gets the top spots — in SHASTA, in the holdings, in the pension funds, in the petrochemical companies, and elsewhere — when it comes to managing the wealthy ministries.

🔹 No matter how you slice it, the relevant minister's team, the President's office team, the First Vice President's team, teams tied to security institutions, and so on — each marches to its own beat, trying to install its own people and take out the rival's.

Personally, I don't think Mr. Pezeshkian has enough charisma or leadership strength to manage these conflicts within the government.

But none of these fights and power struggles are new.

🔹 The country's new problem in recent years is the Islamic Consultative Assembly.

As a supervisory body that shouldn't be meddling in the government's internal fights, it now has a speaker who's clearly unhappy with where he is and wants to install his left and right hands, his affiliates and associates, everywhere from the Privatization Organization to the pension fund to the Persian Gulf Holding to a thousand other places — and he himself has become a party to all these fights.

🔹 Just a few days ago, in the middle of the war between the trusts and their mutual exposés, in the middle of the infighting within the government, I heard that Mr. Ghorbanzadeh — a member of the negotiating team and Mr. Ghalibaf's right-hand man — was removed from the board of directors of the Persian Gulf Holding. I guessed right then that the Oil Minister's departure was certain.

🔹 I say this as a friend: in this situation, the Assembly has lost its supervisory function, and a new party has been added to the government's internal fights, draining its energy.

The Islamic Republic 🇮🇷 executed Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raeisi, two defendants in the "Alikhani Isfahan" case. Coinciding with the start of the World Week Against the Death Penalty, the judiciary of the Islamic Republic executed Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raeisi, two of those arrested during the nationwide protests of Dey 1404, in the case known as "Alikhani Square." These two protesters were executed today, Monday 13 Mehr 1405, in Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan. Shahrzad Shahbazi, a lawyer and the defense attorney for Alireza Sepahi, wrote in this regard: "Alireza Sepahi's retrial was granted by the Supreme Court, but the parallel branch (Branch Two) of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court, without holding a hearing, rejected the retrial in less than 48 hours." Alireza Sepahi had previously been scheduled to be executed in the early hours of Tuesday, 6 Mordad 1405, along with Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani and Amirhossein Safari Hosseinabadi, but before being transferred to the execution site, he suffered a stroke and was taken to the hospital due to the severity of his physical condition. Two days later, after receiving medical treatment, he was returned to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan. Published evidence regarding cases related to the Dey 1404 protesters shows that the death sentences issued so far have been accompanied by serious legal and juridical ambiguities, and in the vast majority of cases, the fundamental principles of a fair trial — including the right to effective access to a lawyer, public proceedings, independent examination of evidence, and full observance of the guarantees stipulated in the Code of Criminal Procedure — have not been observed. Therefore, the issuance and execution of death sentences against protesters, rather than being a sign of an independent and impartial judicial process, indicates that the death penalty has been turned into a tool for creating fear and terror in society and preventing the recurrence of protests. dadban4@mamlekate

An ordinary day! Yesterday I went to one of the public hospitals in central Tehran for an MRI. Even though I had booked an appointment in person in advance, I still waited two hours for my turn. During those two hours of waiting, verbal altercations broke out three times between hospital staff and patients or their companions, one of which nearly turned into a physical fight and made the atmosphere tense. Neither side in the disputes was at fault. Patients and their companions were demanding speed, accuracy, and respect, while the staff—due to the enormous volume and pressure of work on the one hand, and presumably low and inadequate wages on the other—had no patience for hearing complaints, and things escalated to disrespect and verbal altercation! If you sat and listened to the grievances of either side, you would acknowledge that they were right! This is not an exceptional situation in a public healthcare setting. It has become a completely ordinary matter. In some places, it even leads to physical fights, beatings, and sometimes murder. For God's sake, is this even a life? Let those who favor the continuation of sanctions, siege, and war answer! They, of course, do not consider sanctions, siege, and war to be a factor in creating these kinds of problems, and believe that all these problems stem from the president's inclination to negotiate with America and the failure to promulgate the hijab and chastity law. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

entry.title:
[FarsNA] The consequence of befriending deceivers
🔹A crow, a wolf, and a jackal…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @FarsNA

The consequence of befriending deceivers

🔹A crow, a wolf, and a jackal lived in a thicket alongside a lion, and they got by on the leftovers of his kills.

🔹One day, a camel that had fallen behind from a caravan came to that thicket to graze. When the camel came upon the lion, it bowed, and the lion granted it safety, saying it could live in peace under his protection.

🔹Some time later, the lion was badly wounded in a fight with an elephant, collapsed in his cave, and lost the strength to hunt. The animals around him were left helpless with hunger. The crow, looking for a way out, proposed to his companions that they find a way to get the lion to eat the camel.

🔹The jackal said, "The lion has granted him safety, and breaking one's word is shameful." The crow replied, "Leave it to me; I'll devise a scheme so the camel himself walks into being sacrificed."

🔹The crow went to the lion and, with smooth talk, won him over and promised to arrange things so that there would be no need to break the covenant.

🔹Then he went to the wolf, the jackal, and the camel and said, "The Sultan's life is in danger; come, let us show our loyalty and offer ourselves. The lion does not eat our flesh, but the custom of service is fulfilled."

🔹They all went to the lion. First the crow stepped forward and offered himself, but the wolf and the jackal cried out, "You're scrawny and your flesh tastes foul!" Then the jackal volunteered, and the others called his flesh stinking. It was the wolf's turn, and they deemed his flesh harmful.

🔹The simple-hearted camel, seeing this staging, thought to himself that if he too made an offer, the companions would, following the same custom as before, come up with some excuse and the lion's protection would hold. So he came forward and said, "My body is a sacrifice for the Sultan; my flesh is pure and will fill everyone." No sooner had he finished speaking than all three animals said with one voice, "He speaks the truth!" and immediately fell upon him and made him their prey.

#حکایت@Farsna

Iran's water crisis is…

📚 Groundwater Governance: Developments and Advances

Iran's water crisis is no longer a matter of the future; we see its signs today in the drying up of wetlands, land subsidence, and the depletion of groundwater reserves. Years of unchecked extraction from aquifers have consumed resources that, for many, may take decades or even centuries to replenish.

The book "Groundwater Governance: Developments and Advances" takes an interdisciplinary look at one of the most important yet least visible aspects of the water crisis: groundwater — resources that remain unseen, yet the lives, agriculture, and food security of communities depend on them.

By examining the experiences of various countries, this book demonstrates that protecting groundwater is not achievable through isolated projects alone; it requires scientific management, sound policymaking, and cooperation among government, local communities, and consumers.

▪️Iran's water crisis, rather than being a crisis of water scarcity, may be a crisis of water management.
